desc:
A single chef must make every dish in dishes, where dishes[i] = [prep, cook]. The chef prepares the dishes one after another with no breaks, starting at time 0, in an order of the chef's choosing. Preparing dish i takes prep time and needs the chef the whole time. As soon as its preparation is done the dish goes into its own oven and takes cook more time; there are enough ovens for all dishes at once, and the chef is free to start preparing the next dish immediately.

Return the earliest time at which all dishes are finished cooking.

dishes = [[2, 5], [3, 1]]  ->  7

Prepare the long-cooking dish first: it is in the oven from time 2 and done at 7, while the second dish is prepared during 2..5 and done at 6. The other order ends at 10.
hints: The chef's own work always ends at the same moment, the sum of all prep times. Only the cooking tails differ.
Dish i is done at (time its prep ends) + cook_i. Which dishes should get the earliest prep-end times: the ones with long or short cook times?
Prepare dishes in decreasing order of cook time and track max(prep end + cook) over all dishes.
editorial: The finish time is max over dishes of (prep end of the dish + its cook time). The prep ends are the prefix sums of the prep times in the chosen order, so the total prep time is paid by the last dish whichever it is, and the real decision is which dishes get the early finish slots.

Exchange argument: if dish A with a smaller cook time is prepared directly before dish B with a larger cook time, swapping them leaves the end of the pair unchanged, makes B finish earlier, and A's new finish (s + prepB + prepA + cookA) is not larger than B's old finish s + prepA + prepB + cookB. So sort by cook time descending and scan once. Time O(n log n).
solution:
def minFinishTime(dishes):
    t = 0
    best = 0
    for prep, cook in sorted(dishes, key=lambda x: -x[1]):
        t += prep
        best = max(best, t + cook)
    return best
